expectedText:
FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT OF EMPLOYMENT (PROMISSORY FRAUD IN HIRING) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about fraudulent inducement of employment: the situation in which a person accepts a job — and often gives up another one — in reliance on representations by the prospective employer that were false when made. It draws on the Civil Code's codification of deceit and promissory fraud (Civil Code sections 1709, 1710, and 1572) and on the California Supreme Court's decision in Lazar v. Superior Court (Rykoff-Sexton, Inc.) (1996) 12 Cal.4th 631, which holds that a traditional fraud claim for promissory fraud in inducing an employment contract remains available in the employment setting, explains how that claim differs from a misrepresentation used to carry out a termination (Hunter v. Up-Right, Inc.), and describes the kinds of damages such a claim can and cannot reach. It also summarizes Civil Code section 3294, the exemplary-damages statute that Lazar identifies as available in such an action, including its separate rule for when an employer answers in exemplary damages for the acts of its employees. Where a specific employer and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. This sheet is a companion to this corpus's information sheet on Labor Code sections 970 through 972 (the statutory misdemeanor and double-damages remedy for inducing a change of residence for work through knowingly false representations), which is a separate remedy that Lazar itself pleaded alongside the common-law fraud claim described here, and to the corpus's information sheet on the at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contract limits, which addresses the contract side of the same employment relationship. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular recruiting statement, offer, or reliance on an offer gives rise to a claim, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

THE STATUTORY BASIS: DECEIT AND PROMISSORY FRAUD IN THE CIVIL CODE (SECTIONS 1709, 1710, AND 1572)
California codified the tort of deceit in 1872. Civil Code section 1709 makes one who willfully deceives another with intent to induce that person to alter his position to his injury or risk liable for any damage the deceived person thereby suffers. Section 1710 defines a deceit within the meaning of section 1709 as any one of four things: (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the assertion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who has no reasonable ground for believing it to be true; (3) the suppression of a fact by one who is bound to disclose it, or who gives information of other facts likely to mislead for want of communication of that fact; or (4) a promise made without any intention of performing it. The fourth category is the statutory source of what the courts call "promissory fraud." A parallel definition appears in the contract provisions of the Civil Code: section 1572 defines "actual fraud" as any of several acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, with intent to deceive another party or to induce him to enter into the contract, and its fourth category is likewise a promise made without any intention of performing it. As the other clauses of this sheet describe, the California Supreme Court in Lazar v. Superior Court treated these three sections as the Legislature's century-old codification of the common-law action for promissory fraud in inducing a contract, and observed that they contain no express exception for employers or employees.

  Known gap: Sections 1709 and 1710 are quoted in full; section 1572 is quoted only for its introductory clause and its fourth (promise-without-intent) category, and its other four categories are summarized rather than reproduced. These sections state the general law of deceit and fraud and do not mention employment; their application to recruiting representations comes from the case law quoted in the other clauses of this sheet. The related statutory measure-of-damages provision for fraud (Civil Code section 3343, governing fraud in the purchase, sale, or exchange of property) and the general tort damages measure in section 3333 are not restated here. Nothing in these sections addresses negligent misrepresentation as a separate theory (see section 1710, subdivision 2, which the courts treat as its statutory source), the statute of limitations for fraud (Code of Civil Procedure section 338, subdivision (d)), or the heightened pleading standard that the Lazar clause describes.

THE ELEMENTS OF FRAUD, AND WHY A BROKEN HIRING PROMISE CAN BE FRAUD RATHER THAN MERELY BREACH OF CONTRACT (LAZAR V. SUPERIOR COURT)
In Lazar v. Superior Court (Rykoff-Sexton, Inc.) (1996), the California Supreme Court granted review to decide whether, or under what circumstances, a plaintiff may state a cause of action for fraudulent inducement of an employment contract. The court began with the settled elements of fraud, quoting Witkin: (a) misrepresentation (false representation, concealment, or nondisclosure); (b) knowledge of falsity, or scienter; (c) intent to defraud, that is, to induce reliance; (d) justifiable reliance; and (e) resulting damage. It then explained that "promissory fraud" is a subspecies of the action for fraud and deceit: a promise to do something necessarily implies the intention to perform, so where a promise is made without such intention there is an implied misrepresentation of fact that may be actionable fraud, citing Civil Code section 1710, subdivision 4. The court stated that an action for promissory fraud may lie where a defendant fraudulently induces the plaintiff to enter into a contract, and that in such cases the plaintiff's claim does not depend on whether the defendant's promise is ultimately enforceable as a contract — the defrauded party has a cause of action in tort as an alternative to, and in some instances in addition to, a cause of action on the contract. Recovery, the court added, may be limited by the rule against double recovery of tort and contract compensatory damages.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]

Law (9th ed. 1988) Torts, section 676), which was not separately fetched; it is quoted only as reproduced in the opinion. The opinion addresses intentional (promissory) fraud; the plaintiff's separate causes of action for negligent misrepresentation, wrongful termination in violation of public policy, and emotional distress were outside the issue on which review was granted and are not addressed by this clause. The rule against double recovery is stated by reference to Tavaglione v. Billings (1993) 4 Cal.4th 1150, which was not separately fetched.

WHAT RECRUITING REPRESENTATIONS WERE HELD SUFFICIENT TO PLEAD PROMISSORY FRAUD (LAZAR V. SUPERIOR COURT)
The plaintiff in Lazar was the president of a family-owned New York company who was recruited by a California employer over several months. As alleged, he told the recruiter he was concerned about relinquishing a secure job and moving his family, and conditioned his agreement on assurances that the new job would be secure and would involve significant pay increases. The employer allegedly responded that he would continue to be employed so long as he performed his job and achieved goals, that he would have a long-term relationship with the company, that the company was very strong financially with a stable, profitable future, and that his compensation would rise quickly; when he asked for a written contract, he was allegedly told one was unnecessary because "our word is our bond." The complaint alleged that these representations were false when made and known to be false — the company had just experienced its worst economic performance in recent history, was planning a merger that would eliminate the position, secretly intended to treat him as an at-will employee, and had a policy limiting raises to 2 to 3 percent — and that the plaintiff relied on them by resigning his New York position, buying a California home, and moving his family. He was terminated about two years later. The Supreme Court held that these allegations, if true, would establish all the elements of promissory fraud: representations made in order to induce him to come to work in California, falsity, knowledge of falsity at the time the representations were made, and justifiable reliance in leaving secure employment, severing his connections with the New York employment market, uprooting his family, and purchasing a home. The court characterized the complaint as stating a cause of action for promissory fraud "as traditionally understood."

  Known gap: Every fact recited here is an allegation of the complaint, assumed true for purposes of the demurrer; the Supreme Court made no finding that any representation was false or that the employer had the alleged intent, and the opinion does not report the outcome on remand. The opinion involved a recruited executive who relocated across the country; it does not say that any particular category of recruiting statement (for example, a general description of a company's prospects) is or is not actionable, and it does not address representations made to an applicant who did not leave other employment. The plaintiff's separate claim under Labor Code section 970 (inducing a change of residence by misrepresentation) survived the demurrer independently and is addressed in the corpus's separate information sheet on that statute.

FRAUD IN INDUCING EMPLOYMENT VERSUS MISREPRESENTATION USED TO CARRY OUT A TERMINATION (LAZAR EXPLAINING HUNTER V. UP-RIGHT)
The employer in Lazar argued that the Supreme Court's earlier decisions in Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) and Hunter v. Up-Right, Inc. (1993) confined terminated employees to contract damages. Lazar rejected that reading and explained what Hunter actually decided. In Hunter, a welder was falsely told that a corporate decision to eliminate his position had been made and, on that basis, signed a resignation; the Supreme Court concluded that wrongful termination of employment ordinarily does not give rise to a cause of action for fraud or deceit, even if a misrepresentation is used to effect the termination, because the employer could have accomplished the termination directly and the employee therefore could not plead detrimental reliance — the misrepresentation was merely the means to the end the employer desired. Lazar pointed out that Hunter had expressly left open the possibility that a misrepresentation not aimed at effecting termination, but instead designed to induce the employee to alter his or her position detrimentally in some other respect, could support a valid fraud claim even in the context of a wrongful termination, and that all seven justices in Hunter had agreed that the action for promissory fraud remains viable in the employment context. The Lazar court then drew the line that distinguishes the two situations: the misrepresentations alleged in Lazar were made before the employment relationship was formed, when the employer had no coercive power over the applicant and the applicant was free to decline the offered position; the employer could not have compelled him to leave his former job truthfully; and the decision to accept left him in worse circumstances than if he had not been lied to. Because the reliance alleged was truly detrimental, Hunter's core rationale did not apply, and Hunter did not bar the fraud claim.

  Known gap: Hunter v. Up-Right, Inc. (1993) 6 Cal.4th 1174 and Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 654 are described and quoted here only as the Lazar opinion reproduces and characterizes them; neither opinion was separately fetched for this clause, because the CourtListener daily API cap prevented a second independent fetch, and Hunter's own holding should be read from Hunter. Lazar states that its distinction turns on detrimental reliance and on the employer's lack of power to achieve the result without deception; it does not hold that every pre-hire statement is actionable or that every post-hire statement is not, and the court noted that its ruling in Hunter was not meant to alter the law of fraud generally. The opinion's quotation of Hunter's footnote is Hunter's language, not Lazar's.

NO SPECIAL EXEMPTION FOR EMPLOYERS FROM ORDINARY FRAUD RULES, AND THE PARTICULARITY REQUIRED TO PLEAD FRAUD AGAINST A CORPORATE EMPLOYER (LAZAR V. SUPERIOR COURT)
The Lazar court also rejected the argument that the economic-policy reasoning of Foley — which declined to create a new tort remedy for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing in employment — should be extended to restrict traditional fraud remedies when they are sought against an employer. The court observed that Foley concerned whether to recognize a previously unrecognized cause of action, whereas the employer in Lazar was asking the court to restrict tort remedies that already existed. It noted that the Legislature more than a century earlier had codified the common-law cause of action for promissory fraud in inducing a contract, along with the actions for promissory fraud and fraud generally, in Civil Code sections 1572, subdivision 4, 1709, and 1710, and that those statutes provide no express exception for employers or employees; judicial restraint therefore counseled against disallowing the claim. The court stated that Foley does not provide authority for exempting employers from ordinary fraud rules that apply to Californians generally, and that fraudulent inducement of contract is an area that has always involved both contract and tort principles — for example, a party whose contract was secured by fraudulent representations may elect to affirm the contract and sue for the fraud. At the same time, the court emphasized the safeguard built into fraud pleading: in California, fraud must be pled specifically, general and conclusory allegations do not suffice, and a plaintiff asserting fraud against a corporate employer bears an even greater burden, having to allege the names of the persons who made the allegedly fraudulent representations, their authority to speak, to whom they spoke, what they said or wrote, and when it was said or written.

WHAT DAMAGES A FRAUDULENT-INDUCEMENT CLAIM REACHES, AND WHAT MUST BE SOUGHT IN CONTRACT INSTEAD (LAZAR V. SUPERIOR COURT)
Lazar draws a specific line around the damages available on a fraudulent-inducement-of-employment claim. The court explained that, because of the extra measure of blameworthiness inhering in fraud, fraud plaintiffs may recover "out-of-pocket" damages in addition to benefit-of-the-bargain damages, and that a fraudulently hired employee may incur a variety of damages separate from the termination itself, such as the expense and disruption of moving or the loss of security and income associated with former employment. In its conclusion the court stated that, on his fraud claim, the plaintiff could properly seek damages for the costs of uprooting his family, expenses incurred in relocation, and the loss of security and income associated with his former New York employment; that, on the facts as pled, he had to rely on his contract claim to recover any loss of income caused by the wrongful termination of his new employment; and that any overlap between tort and contract damages would be limited by the rule against double recovery. The court summarized that the plaintiff could proceed with his claim for fraud in the inducement of the employment contract, seeking damages for all the detriment proximately caused thereby under Civil Code section 3333, as well as appropriate exemplary damages under Civil Code section 3294.

The opinion does not quantify any category of damages, does not address emotional-distress damages on the fraud claim, and does not discuss mitigation. Later Court of Appeal decisions applying Lazar to measure lost-earnings damages from a former job, and to promissory-estoppel claims where a job offer is withdrawn after the applicant has resigned other employment, were located but could not be independently fetched twice for this sheet because of the CourtListener daily API cap, and are therefore not quoted or relied on here.

EXEMPLARY DAMAGES FOR FRAUD, AND WHEN AN EMPLOYER ANSWERS FOR ITS EMPLOYEES' FRAUD (CIVIL CODE SECTION 3294)
Civil Code section 3294, which Lazar identifies as the source of exemplary damages on a fraudulent-inducement claim, provides in subdivision (a) that in an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff may recover, in addition to actual damages, damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant. Subdivision (c)(3) defines "fraud" for this purpose as an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. Because recruiting representations are typically made by individual managers or recruiters on an employer's behalf, subdivision (b) is directly relevant: an employer is not liable for exemplary damages based on the acts of an employee unless the employer had advance knowledge of the employee's unfitness and employed him or her with a conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others, or authorized or ratified the wrongful conduct, or was personally guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice; and for a corporate employer, that advance knowledge and conscious disregard, authorization, ratification, or act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-11]
  "In an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff, in addition to the actual damages, may recover damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3294(a), Civ. Code § 3294(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3294.)

With respect to a corporate employer, the advance knowledge and conscious disregard, authorization, ratification or act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation."

expectedJSON.body: This information sheet, prepared by Jordan Lee, summarizes what California law says about fraudulent inducement of employment: the situation in which a person accepts a job — and often gives up another one — in reliance on representations by the prospective employer that were false when made. It draws on the Civil Code's codification of deceit and promissory fraud (Civil Code sections 1709, 1710, and 1572) and on the California Supreme Court's decision in Lazar v. Superior Court (Rykoff-Sexton, Inc.) (1996) 12 Cal.4th 631, which holds that a traditional fraud claim for promissory fraud in inducing an employment contract remains available in the employment setting, explains how that claim differs from a misrepresentation used to carry out a termination (Hunter v. Up-Right, Inc.), and describes the kinds of damages such a claim can and cannot reach. It also summarizes Civil Code section 3294, the exemplary-damages statute that Lazar identifies as available in such an action, including its separate rule for when an employer answers in exemplary damages for the acts of its employees. Where a specific employer and jobseeker are named below, those names are Acme, Inc. and Casey Alex; this sheet can also be read on its own, without any specific party named, as a general reference. This sheet is a companion to this corpus's information sheet on Labor Code sections 970 through 972 (the statutory misdemeanor and double-damages remedy for inducing a change of residence for work through knowingly false representations), which is a separate remedy that Lazar itself pleaded alongside the common-law fraud claim described here, and to the corpus's information sheet on the at-will presumption and implied-in-fact contract limits, which addresses the contract side of the same employment relationship. This sheet states the law; it does not evaluate whether any particular recruiting statement, offer, or reliance on an offer gives rise to a claim, and it is not a substitute for individualized legal advice.

California codified the tort of deceit in 1872. Civil Code section 1709 makes one who willfully deceives another with intent to induce that person to alter his position to his injury or risk liable for any damage the deceived person thereby suffers. Section 1710 defines a deceit within the meaning of section 1709 as any one of four things: (1) the suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; (2) the assertion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who has no reasonable ground for believing it to be true; (3) the suppression of a fact by one who is bound to disclose it, or who gives information of other facts likely to mislead for want of communication of that fact; or (4) a promise made without any intention of performing it. The fourth category is the statutory source of what the courts call "promissory fraud." A parallel definition appears in the contract provisions of the Civil Code: section 1572 defines "actual fraud" as any of several acts committed by a party to a contract, or with his connivance, with intent to deceive another party or to induce him to enter into the contract, and its fourth category is likewise a promise made without any intention of performing it. As the other clauses of this sheet describe, the California Supreme Court in Lazar v. Superior Court treated these three sections as the Legislature's century-old codification of the common-law action for promissory fraud in inducing a contract, and observed that they contain no express exception for employers or employees.

A deceit, within the meaning of the last section, is either: 1. The suggestion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who does not believe it to be true; 2. The assertion, as a fact, of that which is not true, by one who has no reasonable ground for believing it to be true; 3. The suppression of a fact, by one who is bound to disclose it, or who gives information of other facts which are likely to mislead for want of communication of that fact; or, 4. A promise, made without any intention of performing it.

Actual fraud, within the meaning of this Chapter, consists in any of the following acts, committed by a party to the contract, or with his connivance, with intent to deceive another party thereto, or to induce him to enter into the contract:

expectedJSON.body: In Lazar v. Superior Court (Rykoff-Sexton, Inc.) (1996), the California Supreme Court granted review to decide whether, or under what circumstances, a plaintiff may state a cause of action for fraudulent inducement of an employment contract. The court began with the settled elements of fraud, quoting Witkin: (a) misrepresentation (false representation, concealment, or nondisclosure); (b) knowledge of falsity, or scienter; (c) intent to defraud, that is, to induce reliance; (d) justifiable reliance; and (e) resulting damage. It then explained that "promissory fraud" is a subspecies of the action for fraud and deceit: a promise to do something necessarily implies the intention to perform, so where a promise is made without such intention there is an implied misrepresentation of fact that may be actionable fraud, citing Civil Code section 1710, subdivision 4. The court stated that an action for promissory fraud may lie where a defendant fraudulently induces the plaintiff to enter into a contract, and that in such cases the plaintiff's claim does not depend on whether the defendant's promise is ultimately enforceable as a contract — the defrauded party has a cause of action in tort as an alternative to, and in some instances in addition to, a cause of action on the contract. Recovery, the court added, may be limited by the rule against double recovery of tort and contract compensatory damages.

citations.quote: whether or under what circumstances a plaintiff may state a cause of action for fraudulent inducement of employment contract. The Court of Appeal concluded the allegations of the plaintiff in this case are adequate to state such a cause of action. For the reasons that follow, we agree.

citations.cite: 12 Cal. 4th 631, 638 (1996) (quoting 5 Witkin, Summary of Cal. Law (9th ed. 1988) Torts, § 676, p. 778)
citations.quote: The elements of fraud, which give rise to the tort action for deceit, are (a) misrepresentation (false representation, concealment, or nondisclosure); (b) knowledge of falsity (or ‘scienter’); (c) intent to defraud, i.e., to induce reliance; (d) justifiable reliance; and (e) resulting damage.

“Promissory fraud” is a subspecies of the action for fraud and deceit. A promise to do something necessarily implies the intention to perform; hence, where a promise is made without such intention, there is an implied misrepresentation of fact that may be actionable fraud.
An action for promissory fraud may lie where a defendant fraudulently induces the plaintiff to enter into a contract.
In such cases, the plaintiff’s claim does not depend upon whether the defendant’s promise is ultimately enforceable as a contract.
Recovery, however, may be limited by the rule against double recovery of tort and contract compensatory damages.

expectedJSON.body: The plaintiff in Lazar was the president of a family-owned New York company who was recruited by a California employer over several months. As alleged, he told the recruiter he was concerned about relinquishing a secure job and moving his family, and conditioned his agreement on assurances that the new job would be secure and would involve significant pay increases. The employer allegedly responded that he would continue to be employed so long as he performed his job and achieved goals, that he would have a long-term relationship with the company, that the company was very strong financially with a stable, profitable future, and that his compensation would rise quickly; when he asked for a written contract, he was allegedly told one was unnecessary because "our word is our bond." The complaint alleged that these representations were false when made and known to be false — the company had just experienced its worst economic performance in recent history, was planning a merger that would eliminate the position, secretly intended to treat him as an at-will employee, and had a policy limiting raises to 2 to 3 percent — and that the plaintiff relied on them by resigning his New York position, buying a California home, and moving his family. He was terminated about two years later. The Supreme Court held that these allegations, if true, would establish all the elements of promissory fraud: representations made in order to induce him to come to work in California, falsity, knowledge of falsity at the time the representations were made, and justifiable reliance in leaving secure employment, severing his connections with the New York employment market, uprooting his family, and purchasing a home. The court characterized the complaint as stating a cause of action for promissory fraud "as traditionally understood."

citations.quote: In response to Lazar’s concerns, Rykoff made representations to Lazar that led him to believe he would continue to be employed by Rykoff so long as he performed his job and achieved goals.
Lazar asked for a written employment contract, but was refused. Rykoff stated a written contract was unnecessary because “our word is our bond.”

Rykoff’s representations to Lazar regarding the terms on which he would be retained, Rykoff’s financial health and Lazar’s potential compensation were false and, when making them, Rykoff’s agents knew they were false.

Lazar’s allegations, if true, would establish all the elements of promissory fraud. As detailed above, Lazar alleges that, in order to induce him to come to work in California, Rykoff intentionally represented to him he would be employed by the company so long as he performed his job, he would receive significant increases in salary, and the company was strong financially. Lazar further alleges that Rykoff’s representations were false, and he justifiably relied on them in leaving secure New York employment, severing his connections with the New York employment market, uprooting his family, purchasing a California home and moving here.
These allegations adequately state a cause of action for promissory fraud as traditionally understood.

The plaintiff's separate claim under Labor Code section 970 (inducing a change of residence by misrepresentation) survived the demurrer independently and is addressed in the corpus's separate information sheet on that statute.

expectedJSON.body: The employer in Lazar argued that the Supreme Court's earlier decisions in Foley v. Interactive Data Corp. (1988) and Hunter v. Up-Right, Inc. (1993) confined terminated employees to contract damages. Lazar rejected that reading and explained what Hunter actually decided. In Hunter, a welder was falsely told that a corporate decision to eliminate his position had been made and, on that basis, signed a resignation; the Supreme Court concluded that wrongful termination of employment ordinarily does not give rise to a cause of action for fraud or deceit, even if a misrepresentation is used to effect the termination, because the employer could have accomplished the termination directly and the employee therefore could not plead detrimental reliance — the misrepresentation was merely the means to the end the employer desired. Lazar pointed out that Hunter had expressly left open the possibility that a misrepresentation not aimed at effecting termination, but instead designed to induce the employee to alter his or her position detrimentally in some other respect, could support a valid fraud claim even in the context of a wrongful termination, and that all seven justices in Hunter had agreed that the action for promissory fraud remains viable in the employment context. The Lazar court then drew the line that distinguishes the two situations: the misrepresentations alleged in Lazar were made before the employment relationship was formed, when the employer had no coercive power over the applicant and the applicant was free to decline the offered position; the employer could not have compelled him to leave his former job truthfully; and the decision to accept left him in worse circumstances than if he had not been lied to. Because the reliance alleged was truly detrimental, Hunter's core rationale did not apply, and Hunter did not bar the fraud claim.

all seven members of the court either expressly or impliedly agreed that the action for promissory fraud remains viable in the employment context.

Rykoff’s misrepresentations were made before the employment relationship was formed, when Rykoff had no coercive power over Lazar and Lazar was free to decline the offered position.

In sum, Hunter’s core rationale (that a substantial fraud claim could not be pled because the element of detrimental reliance was absent) does not apply to this case. As alleged, Lazar’s reliance was truly detrimental.

(1988) 47 Cal.3d 654 are described and quoted here only as the Lazar opinion reproduces and characterizes them; neither opinion was separately fetched for this clause, because the CourtListener daily API cap prevented a second independent fetch, and Hunter's own holding should be read from Hunter. Lazar states that its distinction turns on detrimental reliance and on the employer's lack of power to achieve the result without deception; it does not hold that every pre-hire statement is actionable or that every post-hire statement is not, and the court noted that its ruling in Hunter was not meant to alter the law of fraud generally. The opinion's quotation of Hunter's footnote is Hunter's language, not Lazar's.

expectedJSON.body: The Lazar court also rejected the argument that the economic-policy reasoning of Foley — which declined to create a new tort remedy for breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing in employment — should be extended to restrict traditional fraud remedies when they are sought against an employer. The court observed that Foley concerned whether to recognize a previously unrecognized cause of action, whereas the employer in Lazar was asking the court to restrict tort remedies that already existed. It noted that the Legislature more than a century earlier had codified the common-law cause of action for promissory fraud in inducing a contract, along with the actions for promissory fraud and fraud generally, in Civil Code sections 1572, subdivision 4, 1709, and 1710, and that those statutes provide no express exception for employers or employees; judicial restraint therefore counseled against disallowing the claim. The court stated that Foley does not provide authority for exempting employers from ordinary fraud rules that apply to Californians generally, and that fraudulent inducement of contract is an area that has always involved both contract and tort principles — for example, a party whose contract was secured by fraudulent representations may elect to affirm the contract and sue for the fraud. At the same time, the court emphasized the safeguard built into fraud pleading: in California, fraud must be pled specifically, general and conclusory allegations do not suffice, and a plaintiff asserting fraud against a corporate employer bears an even greater burden, having to allege the names of the persons who made the allegedly fraudulent representations, their authority to speak, to whom they spoke, what they said or wrote, and when it was said or written.

(See Civ. Code, §§ 1572, subd. 4, 1709, 1710.) These statutes provide no express exception for employers or employees.
In California, fraud must be pled specifically; general and conclusory allegations do not suffice.

expectedJSON.body: Lazar draws a specific line around the damages available on a fraudulent-inducement-of-employment claim. The court explained that, because of the extra measure of blameworthiness inhering in fraud, fraud plaintiffs may recover "out-of-pocket" damages in addition to benefit-of-the-bargain damages, and that a fraudulently hired employee may incur a variety of damages separate from the termination itself, such as the expense and disruption of moving or the loss of security and income associated with former employment. In its conclusion the court stated that, on his fraud claim, the plaintiff could properly seek damages for the costs of uprooting his family, expenses incurred in relocation, and the loss of security and income associated with his former New York employment; that, on the facts as pled, he had to rely on his contract claim to recover any loss of income caused by the wrongful termination of his new employment; and that any overlap between tort and contract damages would be limited by the rule against double recovery. The court summarized that the plaintiff could proceed with his claim for fraud in the inducement of the employment contract, seeking damages for all the detriment proximately caused thereby under Civil Code section 3333, as well as appropriate exemplary damages under Civil Code section 3294.

Lazar, therefore, may proceed with his claim for fraud in the inducement of employment contract, properly seeking damages for “all the detriment proximately caused thereby” (Civ. Code, § 3333), as well as appropriate exemplary damages (Civ. Code, § 3294).

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code section 3294, which Lazar identifies as the source of exemplary damages on a fraudulent-inducement claim, provides in subdivision (a) that in an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff may recover, in addition to actual damages, damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant. Subdivision (c)(3) defines "fraud" for this purpose as an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury. Because recruiting representations are typically made by individual managers or recruiters on an employer's behalf, subdivision (b) is directly relevant: an employer is not liable for exemplary damages based on the acts of an employee unless the employer had advance knowledge of the employee's unfitness and employed him or her with a conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others, or authorized or ratified the wrongful conduct, or was personally guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice; and for a corporate employer, that advance knowledge and conscious disregard, authorization, ratification, or act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation.

citations.quote: In an action for the breach of an obligation not arising from contract, where it is proven by clear and convincing evidence that the defendant has been guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice, the plaintiff, in addition to the actual damages, may recover damages for the sake of example and by way of punishing the defendant.

An employer shall not be liable for damages pursuant to subdivision (a), based upon acts of an employee of the employer, unless the employer had advance knowledge of the unfitness of the employee and employed him or her with a conscious disregard of the rights or safety of others or authorized or ratified the wrongful conduct for which the damages are awarded or was personally guilty of oppression, fraud, or malice. With respect to a corporate employer, the advance knowledge and conscious disregard, authorization, ratification or act of oppression, fraud, or malice must be on the part of an officer, director, or managing agent of the corporation.

“Fraud” means an intentional misrepresentation, deceit, or concealment of a material fact known to the defendant with the intention on the part of the defendant of thereby depriving a person of property or legal rights or otherwise causing injury.
